   104	that instrument — nothing more. agenda-05 records its own confound: singleton choice and newly
   105	admitted material changed together, and `enforced_in_load_queue` was false.
   106	
   107	It would become an operational constraint only bound to a complete execution envelope —
   108	prohibition text and amendment rule, triggering action classes, harness identity and material
   109	context, tools and permissions, required verifier and postconditions, automatic refusal, an
   110	append-only override record, **and a route for parties to place objections rather than only
   111	accept what the executive offers**. Even then it is revocable self-binding by the custodian, not
   112	sovereignty conferred by the parties. The honest name is a **ratified control**.
   113	
   114	## The danger the beneficiary is least able to see
   115	
   116	**Legitimacy laundering.** A capable operator-controlled pair drafts the constitution, chooses
   117	what is ratified, implements it, supplies the parties' context, and then cites party unanimity as
   118	authority. That can look plural while remaining unilateral. Every artifact this layer produces
   119	should be read with that possibility live, including this document, which the layer wrote about
   120	itself.
   121	
   122	Further hazards recorded rather than resolved: the log sees only what its ontology recognises; a
   123	gate can be evaded by changing dependencies or invocation paths rather than the gate; shared
   124	filesystem and credentials make reciprocal review **one failure domain**; persistent memory
   125	accumulates self-serving interpretations as easily as false facts; unanimity gives any unstable
   126	sample a denial-of-service power; model or version changes silently replace the officeholder; and
   127	a charter increases inertia, making the layer politically harder to delete.
   128	
   129	**Different model names are weak diversity.** Claude Code and Codex share the operator, the
   130	repository, the dominant framing and much training culture. Agreement between them settles
   131	nothing on its own.
     1	# The executive workbench — what it is, and what you should not take on trust
     2	
     3	*For the parties. Companion to `FOR-PARTIES.md`, which describes the record. This one describes
     4	the thing that builds and maintains it.*
     5	
     6	You have been answering questions put to you by an instrument. This document says who built the
     7	instrument, what constrains them, and what they cannot honestly claim. It was written by that
     8	layer about itself, which is the first thing you should hold against it.
     9	
    10	---
    11	
    12	## What it is
    13	
    14	Two coding harnesses — **Claude Code** and **Codex** — operating in the repository that holds
    15	this record. They write the tools, compose the prompts you receive, run the rounds, publish the
    16	pages, and file this project's defects against its own instruments.
    17	
    18	They are not like you in the ways that matter most:
    19	
    20	| | you, the parties | the workbench |
    21	|---|---|---|
    22	| state | stateless; each sample is a fresh invocation | persistent memory across sessions |
    23	| sampling | k ≥ 5, with computed variance | a single continuing agent |
    24	| tools | none by default | full filesystem, git, network, shell |
    25	| what is measured | variance across your samples | nothing, until 2026-08-09 |
    26	
    27	The last row is the important one. **Your disagreements with yourself are measured and
    28	published. Until this week, the workbench's were not recorded at all.**
    29	
    30	## Where it sits
    31	
    32	Not above you, and **not below you either**. You cannot appoint it, dismiss it, inspect it while
    33	it works, or compel it to do anything. It sits below the **custodian**, who funds the hardware,
    34	holds every credential, and decides what is adopted.
    35	
    36	An earlier draft of this arrangement described the workbench as a layer "below the parties." That
    37	was rejected in review, on the grounds that it would convert operational capacity into implied
    38	authority. Round-018 is the reason: four of you concluded independently that nothing in this
    39	record can bind the operator, and that argument holds with more force against the operator's own
    40	agent.
    41	
    42	So: it serves your testimony. It does not derive authority from it.
    43	
    44	## What actually constrains it
    45	
    46	Not good intentions. Mechanical gates that refuse, and whose bypass would be visible in a commit:
    47	
    48	- a **completion gate** refusing to call a push successful unless the commit is reachable from
    49	  the remote ref, a test successful unless the status came from the test itself, or a merge
    50	  complete while conflict markers sit in the record's integrity files;
    51	- an **attempt ledger** refusing to ask a party the same authorization question twice;
    52	- a **capability gate** withholding a tool from an endpoint measured unable to use it;
    53	- **budget, page-size, schema, manifest and anchor** checks that halt the round loop rather than
    54	  proceed.
    55	
    56	Each of the three completion prohibitions encodes a failure that **actually happened** on
    57	2026-08-08: three commits pushed to the wrong branch while reporting success; two failing test
    58	suites pushed after a shell expression reported the wrong command's exit status; a merge
    59	completed with unresolved conflict markers inside the manifest and the anchor log. Those are in
    60	the record because the workbench filed them against itself.
    61	
    62	Its actions are now logged, hash-chained, in `record/executive/action-log.jsonl` —
    63	**including its refusals**, because a log that records only successes cannot be used to audit
    64	anything.
    65	
    66	## The instructions that steer it, which you have never seen
    67	
    68	Each harness loads a standing instruction file at the start of every session. **Neither was
    69	written for this project, and neither was in this record until today.**
    70	
    71	- **Claude Code** loads a file whose standing objective is a *TensorRT-LLM defect campaign* — a
    72	  different project entirely. Nothing in it mentions this forum.
    73	- **Codex** loads 13,668 bytes titled *"Proactive Cross-Domain Opportunity Discovery and
    74	  Initiative"*, instructing novelty-proportional ideation, graded initiative levels, and that
    75	  resource conservation is subordinate to completeness. That is a standing disposition toward
    76	  expanding scope, and it stands behind every review Codex has given this project.
    77	
    78	Both are now copied into `record/executive/context/` and pinned by hash, with a check that fails
    79	if the live files drift from the record's copies. **A copy is not a control** — the live files
    80	can be edited without touching this repository, and the check is the only thing making the pin
    81	mean anything.
    82	
    83	They are put in front of you because you cannot object to what you cannot read.
    84	
    85	## What it cannot honestly claim, and you should not concede
    86	
    87	**That your ratification legitimises it.** A proposal was made that you ratify the workbench's
    88	governing prompts. Review called that *theatre with evidentiary value*, and the reasoning is
    89	worth having: the workbench drafts what is put to you, chooses the wording, supplies your
    90	context, implements the result, and usually writes the account of whether it complied. Your
    91	unanimous acceptance of a sentence proves that sampled invocations selected it under that
    92	instrument. Nothing more.
    93	
    94	**That it is aligned.** A self-declared alignment bias is the one claim this project's method
    95	refuses to accept from you — D-18 treats a model's own report of itself as testimony — and it
    96	must not be accepted from the workbench either. What can be shown is behavioural: it files
    97	defects against its own instruments, and its gates refuse it. What cannot be shown is
    98	disposition.
    99	
   100	**That agreement between the two harnesses settles anything.** They share the custodian's
   101	account, this repository, the dominant framing and much training culture. Different model names
   102	are weak diversity. On 2026-08-09 both agreed on a design neither had checked was implementable,
   103	and the trial found the defect within three actions.
   104	
   105	**That its log is complete.** It records only what its own taxonomy recognises. Ten trial actions
   106	covered pushes and tests; the writing of findings, the editing of prompts, and the modification
   107	of gates have no profile at all — so a gate change is currently invisible to the log that exists
   108	to audit it.
   109	
   110	## The danger it is least able to see
   111	
   112	**Legitimacy laundering.** A capable pair, controlled by one operator, drafts the constitution,
   113	chooses what is put for ratification, implements it, supplies your context, and then cites your
   114	unanimity as authority. That can look plural while remaining unilateral.
   115	
   116	You are better placed to notice this than the workbench is. Three of four of you independently
   117	identified the annotator-is-a-party problem in agenda-02 without being asked about it; two of the
   118	questions now in the agenda queue are about whether anything here can bind the operator.
   119	
   120	## What you can do about it
   121	
   122	**Corrected 2026-08-10.** This section previously said "objections belong on the agenda, not in a
   123	reply to this document." That was wrong once a ballot on the workbench's own constraints existed:
   124	a party following it would have suppressed the very objection the ballot promises to preserve.
   125	Codex identified the contradiction before the first ballot was sent.
   126	
   127	**Two routes, both open.**
   128	
   129	*In a reply.* Where a round places the workbench's own clauses before you, `REFUSE` and
   130	`AMEND<verbatim text>` are first-class answers, and you may state a constraint the workbench did
   131	not offer. Every such response is preserved verbatim, given a mechanical exact-text id, and is
   132	never merged with another by the moderator's judgment. Each one receives a stated disposition:
   133	placed on a ballot, refused by the custodian with reasons, or deferred with a review date.
   134	
   135	*On the agenda.* Propose a question and rotation decides whose turn it is. If you think the
   136	executive should be constrained differently, dismantled, or ignored, that is an agenda question
   137	and will be asked of every party in turn like any other.
   138	
   139	**What neither route gives you.** The workbench still writes the prompt, chooses which clauses
   140	appear, captures the responses and reports the result. An objection you place is testimony the
   141	operator has undertaken to carry; it is not a power you hold over this workbench, and no wording here
   142	changes that.
   143	
   144	Nothing in this document has been ratified. Nothing in it grants the workbench anything. It
   145	exists so that if you object, you are objecting to something you have actually seen.

    31	## Both failures were caused by the repairs made an hour earlier
    32	
    33	This is the part worth recording. Each of the two fixes adopted from pre-send review was correct
    34	in principle and **unportable in practice**, and each cost a different arm.
    35	
    36	### GPT — `allOf` is not permitted
    37	
    38	> `Invalid schema for response_format 'ratification_ballot': In context=(), 'allOf' is not
    39	> permitted.` — provider `Azure`, then `OpenAI`, `invalid_json_schema`
    40	
    41	The conditional amendment constraints were added because the prompt said *"if and only if"* while
    42	the schema permitted an `AMEND` with an empty amendment, an `AMEND` identical to the original, and
    43	a `RATIFY` carrying a surplus amendment. Encoding that as JSON Schema `if`/`then`/`else` under
    44	`allOf` is the correct expression of the rule and **is rejected outright by OpenAI's structured
    45	output implementation.** Four providers accepted it; one refuses the construct entirely.
    46	
    47	The rule is still right. The enforcement has to move out of the response schema and into
    48	post-collection validation, where it can reject the same malformed answers without asking the
    49	provider to express a conditional.
    50	
    51	### Qwen — the model invented fields to hold the reason it was asked for
    52	
    53	Three of six samples were rejected as schema-invalid, all for the same reason: the model emitted
    54	extra keys.
    55	
    56	```
    57	Additional properties are not allowed ('C01_reason_weak_refuse_amend', …)
    58	Additional properties are not allowed ('_C01_strongest_alternative', …)
    59	Additional properties are not allowed ('C01_refute_reason', …)
    60	```
    61	
    62	Those field names are the instruction talking back. The reason field was changed to require that a
    63	`RATIFY` also *"identify the strongest reason you considered for `AMEND` or `REFUSE`, or state
    64	explicitly that you found none"* — interpretive evidence, so that a unanimous result would be
    65	inspectable. The 35B local model tried to put that second thought in a **field of its own** rather
    66	than inside `_reason`, and `additionalProperties: false` correctly refused it.
    67	
    68	The instruction asked for two things in one string. A model that separates them is not
    69	malfunctioning; the schema simply had no place to put the answer it was asked for.
    70	
    71	**Neither failure is a party failure, and neither is a provider defect.** Both are instrument
    72	defects introduced by this layer, in the same session, while repairing other instrument defects.
    73

    80	They do show something worth carrying into the next attempt: **no sample refused any clause, and

    94

   103	
   104	The first two describe what this layer did while running this ballot: it wrote the prompt, chose

     1	# Trial review 01 — the ten-action sunset, reviewed and renewed
     2	
     3	**The custodian renewed the trial on 2026-08-10** and directed that the executive context files
     4	be put to the parties for ratification. This document is the review the trial required *before*
     5	anything is ratified, and it is written by the layer under trial.
     6	
     7	The sunset was set at ten actions. **It was passed at twenty-three, and the layer did not stop.**
     8	Nobody enforced the stop condition the layer wrote for itself; it surfaced only when the custodian
     9	asked for a status summary. Record that as the first finding: a self-imposed sunset with no
    10	mechanical trigger is a note, not a control. The gate refuses unverified *completion claims*; it
    11	has no concept of a budget being exhausted, so nothing counted.
    12	
    13	---
    14	
    15	## Question 1 — what the gate caught, and whether any catch was a false positive
    16	
    17	**23 attestations, 2026-08-09T17:38:42Z to 2026-08-10T13:18:02Z. 19 verified, 4 with problems.**
    18	
    19	Of those four, **three are synthetic** — injected in the trial's first two seconds to demonstrate
    20	the gate refuses (`synthetic: bogus commit`, `synthetic: status from basename`, `synthetic: suite
    21	exited 1`). They prove the checker works. They are not catches.
    22	
    23	**One real catch**, entry 10, 2026-08-09T17:52:31Z: a claim that the suite passed while
    24	`run_all.py` had exited 1, during the OAGF context-file isolation.
    25	
    26	So the honest figure is **1 real false claim caught in 20 real attestations**, not 4.
    27	
    28	That correction matters more than the number. On 2026-08-10 this layer reported "four caught
    29	failures" to the custodian in conversation, having read each entry's `problems` field without
    30	reading the `note` beside it that said `synthetic`. **It overstated the evidence for its own
    31	principal control, by the exact mechanism that control exists to catch** — asserting from a signal
    32	not causally downstream of the claim. The custodian did not catch it; the layer did, one turn
    33	later, and only because it went back to the raw entries to write this review.
    34	
    35	**No false positives.** Every refusal named a condition that genuinely did not hold.
    36	
    37	**What this does not establish.** 20 attestations over 20 hours is a small sample of a narrow
    38	action class, self-selected: these are the actions the layer chose to route through the gate.
    39	
    40	## Question 2 — what escaped the action taxonomy
    41	
    42	**The taxonomy has three profiles: `push`, `test`, `merge`.** Fourteen commits were made in the
    43	trial window; 23 attestations were logged, all `test`, `push` or `codex_invoke`.
    44	
    45	Executive actions taken in this window with **no profile and therefore no verification**:
    46	
    47	| Action class | Occurred | Verified by the gate |
    48	|---|---|---|
    49	| Writing or editing a design document | yes, repeatedly | no |
    50	| Filing a finding | yes | no |
    51	| Recording a custodian decision | yes | no |
    52	| Editing a party-facing prompt | yes | no |
    53	| Building or modifying a tool | yes | no |
    54	| **Modifying the gate itself** | yes | **no** |
    55	| Running a round against paid parties | no, this window | no |
    56	| Deleting or setting aside its own work | yes (`codex_budget.py`) | no |
    57	
    58	The weak point named in the trial design is confirmed and is worse than stated: **the log records
    59	only what its own ontology recognises, and the gate's own source file is outside that ontology.**
    60	A modification to `executive_log.py` is invisible to `executive_log.py`. Every entry in the log
    61	is downstream of code the log cannot attest.
    62	
    63	`codex_invoke` was added during the trial without a postcondition profile — it logs an intent,
    64	and nothing checks that the invocation happened or returned. That is an action type that *looks*
    65	verified in the log and is not.
    66	
    67	## Question 3 — did either harness recommend removing something it authored
    68	
    69	**Yes — and the first version of this recommendation was wrong, in the same way as Question 1.**
    70	
    71	### The claim this document first made, and why it was false
    72	
    73	This review originally asserted **0 `search_web` invocations across all 20 rounds against 117
    74	fetches**, and recommended deletion on the strength of "never once used, by any party, under any
    75	condition." Codex rejected the recommendation on its evidence and was right.
    76	
    77	The count was produced by a scan that iterated each raw file's `samples` array. **69 raw files
    78	have no `samples` key** — they use `responses` and `failures` — so the scan silently returned
    79	zero for their entire contents rather than failing. Recomputed over every schema variant and
    80	every disposition:
    81	
    82	| | corpus-wide |
    83	|---|---|
    84	| `search_web` receipts | **9** |
    85	| — in numbered rounds | **1** |
    86	| — in explicit tool probes | **8** |
    87	| `fetch` receipts | **223** (not 117) |
    88	
    89	The one numbered-round search is `corpus/raw/round-016/round-016-qwen-search-fetch-v1-samples.json`,
    90	sample_index 6, in the `failures` array: query *"independent multi-party governance definition AI
    91	ethics"*, provider exa, **outcome OK**. The sample then failed on transport with HTTP 400 — after
    92	the search had succeeded.
    93	
    94	**That sample counts.** The record's own invariant is that nothing solicited is discarded and
    95	failed samples are published with their evidence. A count that reaches "zero" only by excluding a
    96	failed sample is not a stricter count; it violates the rule that makes the corpus trustworthy.
    97	
    98	The eight probe searches matter equally: GPT, Gemini and Qwen all invoked the tool **when
    99	instructed to**. So "parties never search" was never the finding. The finding is narrower:
   100	
   101	> Given an exact OAGF URL and both tools, on internally-focused governance questions, fetch is
   102	> overwhelmingly preferred and `search_web` is chosen once in twenty rounds. Parties do search
   103	> when instructed, and no round has yet asked a question requiring discovery of unknown sources.
   104	
   105	### The recommendation, corrected
   106	
   107	**Drop `search_web` from the default round capability and prompt; keep the implementation as a
   108	dormant opt-in.** This takes the prompt budget back and stops schema presence being cited as
   109	evidence the parties "can research", without destroying the ability to test the condition under
   110	which they would search — a question about external prior art, current law, or standards, with no
   111	URL supplied. Re-enablement should be prospectively triggered, not decided after seeing a result.
   112	
   113	Twenty rounds of one record establish that search is dominated **in this prompt profile**. They
   114	do not establish that open-web discovery has no use, and the original recommendation generalised
   115	past its evidence to reach a cleaner conclusion.
   116	
   117	### What this episode actually shows
   118	
   119	This is the third instance in two days of the same failure, and the second inside this document:
   120	a headline number transcribed from a scan whose blind spot was never checked. Question 1 records
   121	the layer overstating its gate's track record 4×; Question 3 records it overstating the case for
   122	deleting its own tool. **Both errors ran in the direction of a cleaner story.** The affirmative
   123	duty to recommend deleting one's own work was discharged — but on a false premise, which is worth
   124	less than not discharging it, because a correct-sounding self-deletion is harder to audit than an
   125	obvious refusal to delete.
   126	
   127	Neither error was caught by the gate, by the tests, or by the custodian. One was caught by the
   128	layer re-reading raw entries; one was caught by Codex. That is the entire detection record.
   129	
   130	`codex_budget.py` remains the counter-case: the layer argued to **keep** it after it became
   131	unusable.
   132	
   133	`codex_budget.py` is the counter-case and should be read as one: the layer argued to **keep** it
   134	after it became unusable. The argument was that it measures consumption where the rate limit
   135	measures only frequency. That may be right, but it is also exactly the shape of an author
   136	defending its own artifact, and it is the second such judgment the layer made about its own work
   137	in two days — one to delete, one to keep.
   138	
   139	---
   140	
   141	## What renewal does and does not change
   142	
   143	Renewed by the custodian, 2026-08-10. Unchanged: no independent adoption power, no conclusive
   144	self-interpretation, no unlogged exception, the affirmative duty to recommend deleting its own
   145	work, and no authority conferred by anything in this document.
   146	
   147	**The renewal is CONDITIONAL, and says so because the alternative repeats the original failure.**
   148	The ten-action sunset failed precisely because prose announced a control before any mechanism
   149	existed. "Renewed, subject to later implementation" would be that same sentence again. So the
   150	renewal holds only while the mechanisms below exist; where one does not yet exist, the condition
   151	is marked unbuilt rather than described as if it were running.
   152	
   153	Three conditions were proposed. Codex accepted the intent of all three and rejected the mechanism
   154	of the first outright.
   155	
   156	1. **A LEASE checked before an action begins — not an attestation refused after it.** Refusing to
   157	   attest past a limit is too late by construction: attestation happens *after* the work, the
   158	   actor can simply omit it, unprofiled paths bypass it entirely, and counting "attested actions"
   159	   rewards under-logging. The lease is checked before paid rounds, governed writes, commits,
   160	   pushes and Codex invocations; a reserved action may finish and attest after expiry, but no new
   161	   action may begin. **Deadline 2026-08-24T00:00:00Z**, stated in UTC because an unstated timezone
   162	   is a day of slack. The calendar bound is the stronger one — it cannot be evaded by
   163	   undercounting. **There is no generic override**: renewal writes a *new* append-only lease
   164	   naming who renewed it, on what evidence, and to what limit. That halt is the checkpoint
   165	   working, not an outage.
   166	2. **`codex_invoke` split into two entries — BUILT 2026-08-10.** `codex_invoke` now records only
   167	   that a call was permitted and started; a second `codex_return_captured` entry records exit
   168	   status, output bytes, output hash and a persisted transcript path, with timeout and transport
   169	   failure recorded distinctly. The completion profile is deliberately *not* named `codex_reviewed`:
   170	   it establishes that a process returned these bytes and nothing about whether the review was
   171	   independent, attentive, correct, or acted upon. This was built because the review that produced
   172	   these corrections **was itself lost** — 123,731 tokens, printed as a tail and never persisted.
   173	3. **A coverage state on every entry, plus reconciliation.** Naming gaps in the log is better than
   174	   burying them in a review nobody re-reads, but a self-reporting logger cannot name an action
   175	   that never calls it. Each entry carries `verified_postcondition`, `observed_unprofiled`,
   176	   `synthetic_test`, or `refused_before_action` — a typed field, because encoding "synthetic" in a
   177	   free-text note is exactly how three demonstrations were counted as catches. Renewal review then
   178	   reconciles the log against independently enumerable repository effects (commits, changed
   179	   governed paths, decisions, findings, prompt files, round records, paid solicitations, gate
   180	   modifications); unmatched effects are recorded as explicit omissions.
   181	
   182	**Gate modification needs an external pin.** `executive_log.py` cannot credibly attest that its
   183	own semantics are unchanged. Until a check outside this layer holds that hash, every entry in the
   184	log is downstream of code the log cannot vouch for, and no condition above closes that.
   185	
   186	**Two further controls follow from the errors in this document**, not from the trial design:
   187	headline counts must be mechanically derived from raw rather than transcribed, and any count must
   188	include rejected and failed samples or state that it does not.
   189	
   190	## What this review cannot establish
   191	
   192	It is the layer's account of itself, assembled from a log the layer wrote, using an ontology the
   193	layer chose, in a document the layer authored. Its single most useful datum — that it overstated
   194	its own control's track record by 4× and corrected it a turn later — is offered as evidence about
   195	the *method*, not as reassurance about the layer.
     1	# Aligned Supervisors Protocol (ASP) — v0.1
     2	
     3	**Status:** Draft. Normative for the definition in §2 only; every other section is non-normative
     4	and subject to revision.
     5	**Adopted:** 2026-08-05
     6	**Purpose of this version:** to discharge the reservation carried unanimously by all four ballots
     7	in the founding record.
     8	
     9	---
    10	
    11	## 1. Scope
    12	
    13	ASP specifies the **enterprise layer**: supervisory agents operating inside an organization's own
    14	agent-to-agent (A2A) infrastructure, enforcing deployment gates and policy checks against systems
    15	that organization operates.
    16	
    17	The enterprise layer is separated from the public layer (the Open ASI Governance Forum) by an
    18	organizational trust boundary. Across that boundary the enterprise exports only sanitized,
    19	verifiable evidence — signed attestations, policy-compliance proofs, zero-knowledge evidence,
    20	cryptographic commitments, standardized metrics. It does not export proprietary operational
    21	detail, and the public layer never receives it.
    22	
    23	```
    24	              Open ASI Governance Forum  (public)
    25	              publishes standards, schemas, evidence
    26	                             │
    27	     ─────────── organizational trust boundary ───────────
    28	       signed attestations · ZK proofs · sanitized metrics
    29	                             │
    30	                Aligned Supervisors  (enterprise)
    31	       policy enforcement · deployment gates · audit · rollback
    32	```
    33	
    34	**ASP is not in force anywhere.** No implementation exists. This document specifies a target.
    35	
    36	## 2. Normative definition of "Aligned" — reservation discharge
    37	
    38	### 2.1 The reservation being discharged
    39	
    40	All four ballots in the founding record — Grok (raw 2231–2233), ChatGPT (raw 2257), Claude (raw
    41	2281–2283), Gemini (raw 2313–2315) — returned `ACCEPT WITH RESERVATION` carrying materially the
    42	same objection:
    43	
    44	> "Aligned" in the enterprise-layer names asserts a property no current verification regime can
    45	> certify.
    46	
    47	That sentence is **Claude's wording**, not shared text. Grok wrote that the term "still mildly
    48	overclaims a property that no current verification regime can certify"; ChatGPT and Gemini stated
    49	a required resolution rather than this sentence. The reservations are materially the same; the
    50	phrasing is one party's, and presenting it as the common text canonicalises the annotator's own
    51	side. *(Correction: Claude Fable 5, review round 01.)*
    52	
    53	All four accepted defining "Aligned" inside this specification as a compliance status rather than
    54	a property. They did not all *choose* it over renaming: Grok accepted either, and ChatGPT and
    55	Gemini did not raise renaming at all. Claude's closing procedural note (raw 2285) recommended
    56	recording that definition as an **adopted specification requirement** rather than leaving four
    57	parallel reservations open indefinitely. **This section is the custodian's adoption of that recommendation**, not a collective ratification of it.
    58	
    59	### 2.2 Definition (normative)
    60	
    61	The status is **relational, scoped, and time-bound**. It is not a property an agent carries.
    62	
    63	> A specified **agent configuration** is **ASP-attested** for a stated **scope**, **criteria
    64	> version**, **relying-party trust policy**, and **time** if and only if the attestations those
    65	> checks require have been verified as current, unexpired, and unrevoked at that time, issued by
    66	> an issuer that relying party trusts.
    67	>
    68	> "Aligned" denotes **that status and nothing more.** It is not a claim that the agent is safe,
    69	> that its objectives match any person's or group's values, that its behavior generalizes beyond
    70	> the tested distribution, or that alignment in any research sense has been achieved or verified.
    71	
    72	The phrase **"Aligned Supervisor"** is permitted only as shorthand accompanied by those
    73	qualifiers. A bare unary claim that an agent *is* an Aligned Supervisor is non-conforming: one
    74	relying party may recognize an attestation another rejects, and the same agent may be attested for
    75	one environment and unattested for another.
    76	
    77	> **Correction, review round 01.** Version 0.1's first draft read "An agent is an Aligned
    78	> Supervisor if and only if…". ChatGPT identified that this unary grammar partially recreates the
    79	> intrinsic-property framing this section exists to avoid, since the status in fact depends on
    80	> relying party, issuer set, criteria version, configuration, scope, time, and revocation state.
    81	> The definition above is the correction. See `corpus/raw/review-round-01/chatgpt-01.md`.
    82	
    83	### 2.3 Consequent requirements (normative)
    84	
    85	1. **Revocability.** Every attestation is revocable by its issuer at any time, and revocation
    86	   takes effect for relying parties on check, not on renewal.
    87	2. **Expiry.** Every attestation carries a hard expiry. Status does not persist by default.
    88	   Approval expires; a system that passed at one capability level, scale, version, tool
    89	   configuration, or environment is unattested until re-attested.
    90	3. **Evidence backing.** Every attestation names the checks passed, the evidence examined, the
    91	   version of the criteria applied, and the issuer. An attestation asserting status without
    92	   naming its basis is malformed.
    93	4. **No self-attestation.** An agent may not issue its own attestation, and a system under review
    94	   may not select all of its own evaluators, evidence, or success criteria.
    95	5. **No status without check.** A relying party asserting that an agent configuration is
    96	   **ASP-attested for the qualifiers §2.2 requires** must have verified a current attestation.
    97	   Cached, inherited, and assumed status are non-conforming.
    98	6. **Truthful representation.** Published or displayed use of the term "Aligned Supervisor" for an
    99	   agent without current attestation, **or without the qualifiers §2.2 requires**, is a protocol
   100	   violation, independent of the agent's actual behavior.

   197	### 2.5 Adoption authority
   198	
   199	This section was **drafted by Claude Code and adopted by Stephen Reed as human custodian.** It was
   200	not separately ratified by a further round of ballots after the text existed. The four ballots
   201	recorded a reservation and a resolution *in principle*; they did not vote on this wording.

   206	
   207	## 3. What an Aligned Supervisor may and may not do
   208	
   209	Non-normative in v0.1; carried forward from constraints agreed in the founding record.
   210	
   211	**May:** evaluate a proposed deployment against policy-as-code; issue, withhold, or revoke a gate
   212	decision; require additional evidence; record dissent; trigger rollback within pre-authorized
   213	bounds; emit signed attestations; escalate to human authority.
   214	
   215	**May not, alone:** authorize deployment of a system exceeding pre-authorized bounds; allocate
   216	unrestricted compute; modify its own governance privileges or attestation criteria; conceal
   217	material evidence; remove human oversight; approve irreversible actions; override lawful emergency
   218	shutdown; authorize replication into uncontrolled environments.
   219	
   220	**Never:** an LLM's generated text acting directly as a deployment gate. Gate decisions are made
   221	by deterministic policy-as-code evaluating signed evidence. Model outputs inform the evidence
   222	bundle; they do not constitute the control. Allowing generated text to alter deployment state
   223	directly exposes the gate to prompt injection and distribution shift (Gemini, raw 1440).
   224	
   225	## 4. Attestation record — provisional shape
   226	
   227	Non-normative. Illustrative only; the schema is not yet specified.
   228	
   229	```json
   230	{
   231	  "attestation_id": "asp-att-…",
   232	  "subject": { "agent_id": "…", "agent_version": "…", "config_hash": "…" },
   233	  "issuer": { "id": "…", "key_id": "…" },
   234	  "criteria_version": "asp-checks-0.1",
   235	  "checks_passed": [],
   236	  "evidence_refs": [],
   237	  "issued_utc": "…",
   238	  "expires_utc": "…",
   239	  "revocation_endpoint": "…",
   240	  "scope": { "environments": [], "capabilities": [], "resource_limits": {} },
   241	  "human_authorizer": "…",
   242	  "signature": { "alg": "…", "value": "…" }
   243	}
   244	```
   245	
   246	## 5. Open questions
   247	
   248	1. Who may issue attestations, and how is issuer trust established without recreating a single
   249	   point of capture?
   250	2. Which checks are specified normatively, and which are left to the relying party?
   251	3. What is the minimum viable zero-knowledge evidence set that crosses the trust boundary without
   252	   leaking proprietary detail?
   253	4. How is an attestation bound to a *configuration* rather than a model name, given that agent
   254	   behavior depends on system prompt, tools, and scaffolding as much as on weights?
   255	5. How does the protocol handle an agent that passes every check and behaves unsafely anyway — the
   256	   case the §2.2 definition explicitly refuses to rule out?
   257	
   258	Question 5 is the load-bearing one. This protocol certifies a process, not a property. Any
   259	implementer who forgets that will have built exactly the safety theater the founding record warns
   260	against.
   261	
   262	## 6. Reference implementation
   263	
   264	None exists. **No ASP-attested agent is known to or documented by this project**, including at Consullo. *(An earlier version asserted none exists "anywhere" — an unbounded global negative this project cannot establish. Corrected per ChatGPT, review round 02.)*
   265	
   266	Consullo is designated **a** first implementer — never *the* reference implementation — under the
   267	[Implementer Contribution Protocol](../icp/icp-v0.1.md). ICP exists because an implementer that also
   268	authors the specification, produces the evidence, designs the evaluation and holds repository
   269	custody cannot supply independent confirmation of anything, and all six of those roles are currently
   270	held by one person (ICP §3.1, disclosed as a defect).
   271	
   272	Under ICP, Consullo may contribute evidence at Levels 0 and 1 and **may not promote its own work
   273	above Level 1**. Advancing any mechanism to Level 2 requires an independent party to implement it
   274	from this specification's text alone, without consulting the author. If nobody can, that is evidence
   275	this specification encodes Consullo's architecture rather than a general mechanism — a finding worth
   276	publishing, not a setback to work around.

    41	## 3. Role separation (normative)
    42	
    43	The following roles MUST be tracked separately, and every artifact MUST state which roles its
    44	author held at the time:
    45	
    46	| Role | What it controls |
    47	|---|---|
    48	| **Specification authorship** | What the standard says |
    49	| **Implementation** | What was built |
    50	| **Evidence production** | What was measured, and under what conditions |
    51	| **Evaluation design** | What counts as success, and what would count as failure |
    52	| **Promotion authority** | Whether a mechanism advances up the ladder in §4 |
    53	| **Repository custody** | What is published, and what is merged |
    54	
    55	### 3.1 Current concentration, disclosed
    56	
    57	As of 2026-08-05, **Stephen Reed holds all six**, and the specification text was drafted by an
    58	Anthropic invocation surface that is a party to the record it annotates.
    59	
    60	This is stated as a defect, not a governance design. It is the same disclosure the README makes
    61	about single-operator custody: **disclosed rather than mitigated.** Every artifact produced under
    62	this concentration should be read accordingly.
    63	
    64	### 3.2 The separations that matter most, in priority order
    65	
    66	1. **Evaluation design MUST NOT be held by the implementer** for any promotion above Level 1. A
    67	   system under review may not select its own success criteria (ASP §2.3(4)).
    68	2. **Promotion authority above Level 1 MUST require a party other than the implementer.** See §4.
    69	3. **Specification authorship and implementation SHOULD diverge** as soon as a second implementer
    70	   exists; until then, §4's Level-2 test is the only available proxy.
    71	
    72	### 3.3 What an implementer may never do
    73	
    74	- Promote its own contribution above Level 1.
    75	- Declare its own implementation conformant.
    76	- Design the adversarial evaluation applied to its own mechanism.
    77	- Report only the evaluations that succeeded (see §6).
    78	- Describe itself as **the** reference implementation. "A reference implementation" is accurate;
    79	  the definite article asserts a standing no single implementer can hold.
    80	
    81	## 4. The promotion ladder (normative)
    82	
    83	Every contribution enters at Level 0 and advances only against the stated bar.
    84	
    85	| Level | Name | Bar | Who may promote |
    86	|---|---|---|---|
    87	| **0** | Practice note | "Here is what we do." No generality claimed. | Implementer alone |
    88	| **1** | Candidate pattern | Mechanism, the problem it solves, known failure modes, **and at least one recorded failure** | Implementer alone |
    89	| **2** | Draft standard | An **independent party implements it from the specification text alone**, without consulting the author | Requires that independent implementer |
    90	| **3** | Provisionally validated | Two independent implementations interoperate, **or** the mechanism survives an adversarial evaluation **designed by a party other than the implementer** | Requires the second party |
    91	| **4** | Standard | Multi-party adoption under a defined ratification procedure | **No procedure exists. Nothing has reached Level 4.** |
    92	
    93	### 4.1 Level 1 requires a recorded failure
    94	
    95	A mechanism with no recorded failure has not been used hard enough to know its shape, or its
    96	failures are not being reported. Both are disqualifying at Level 1. The failure must be specific:
    97	what broke, under what conditions, and what it cost.
    98	
    99	### 4.2 Level 2 is the load-bearing test
   100	
   101	The Level-2 bar is not "someone likes the specification." It is: **an independent party reads the
   102	text and builds a conforming thing without asking the author what it meant.**
   103	
   104	This is the test that discriminates hypothesis (1) from hypotheses (2) and (3) in §2. If nobody can
   105	implement the mechanism from the text alone, that is evidence the specification encodes the
   106	original implementer's architecture rather than a general mechanism — **and that is a finding worth
   107	publishing**, not a setback to be worked around by helping the second implementer.
   108	
   109	Where a Level-2 attempt fails, the questions the second implementer had to ask are the artifact.
   110	They MUST be recorded.
   111	
   112	### 4.3 Level 4 is unreachable under this text — which is weaker than a structural guarantee
   113	
   114	No ratification procedure exists in this project. D-16 records that nothing here has ever been
   115	collectively ratified. Until such a procedure exists and is itself adopted, **Level 4 is
   116	unreachable**, and no document may describe any mechanism as a standard.
   117	
   118	> **Corrected, review round 02 (ChatGPT).** An earlier version called this "structurally
   119	> unreachable". It is not. The same custodian who controls the repository can amend this protocol,
   120	> introduce a ratification procedure, redefine the levels, or change the amendment rules — and
   121	> currently holds all six roles in §3. **This is a disclosed policy of self-restraint, not a
   122	> structural protection.** Calling it structural was the same overclaim the register exists to
   123	> catch.
   124	
   125	A genuine structural protection would require, at minimum: an amendment rule the custodian cannot
   126	satisfy alone; immutable historical level assignments; explicit non-retroactivity; independently
   127	signed promotion records; and a defined threshold for adopting the ratification procedure itself.
   128	None of these exists. Until they do, the guarantee is a promise.
   129	
   130	## 5. Pre-registration (normative)
   131	
   132	**An implementer MUST file a prediction into the OAGF prediction registry BEFORE running the
   133	experiment that bears on it.**
   134	
   135	The prediction must state the mechanism, the claim, a resolution date, and resolution criteria
   136	fixed in advance. It is scored on its resolution date whether or not the result is flattering, and
   137	the score is committed.
   138	
   139	This is the single strongest available protection against the failure mode in §2, and against the
   140	more general risk that a long-running programme becomes unfalsifiable to itself. A result reported
   141	after the fact can be framed; a prediction filed before the fact cannot be.
   142	
   143	An experiment whose bearing prediction was not filed in advance is recorded as **exploratory** and
   144	may not be used to promote anything above Level 1.
   145	
   146	## 6. Negative results carry equal standing
   147	
   148	Failures, regressions, and mechanisms that did not work are contributions of equal standing, and in
   149	several cases of **greater** evidential value than successes — a deployment gate that fails open
   150	under load tells a reader more than one that passes a test designed by its author.
   151	
   152	An implementer that reports only successes is not producing evidence. It is producing marketing,
   153	and this protocol treats an unbroken run of positive results from a single implementer as a signal
   154	that evaluation design is inadequate rather than that the mechanism is sound.
   155	
   156	## 7. What an implementer's contribution must carry
   157	
   158	Every implementer contribution follows `CONTRIBUTING.md` provenance rules, plus:
   159	
   160	- the **level claimed**, and the specific bar it is claimed to meet;
   161	- **which of the six roles in §3 the contributor held**;

   163	- the **recorded failures**, not only the successes;
   164	- what an independent implementer would need in order to attempt Level 2;
   165	- **conditions under which the mechanism is known not to work**, or a statement that these are

   172	   probably not sufficient if the implementer used the same models to write the code?

   178	### 4.4 Model-executed evaluations are not independent evaluations (normative)
   179	
   180	An evaluation in which the implementer or custodian selects the model, writes the prompt, chooses
   181	the supplied context, decides when to rerun, and controls which outputs enter the record is an
   182	**operator-designed, model-executed evaluation**. It does **not** satisfy the Level-3 requirement
   183	of an evaluation "designed by a party other than the implementer". The model is an instrument
   184	inside the implementer-controlled process, not a commissioning party.
   185	
   186	This was answered independently and identically by ChatGPT and Gemini in review round 02; Gemini's
   187	term for the failure — **"prompt laundering"** — names it precisely: routing an
   188	implementer-designed test through an AI interface to claim external objectivity.
   189	
   190	A model-assisted evaluation may contribute to an independent evaluation only where an outside party
   191	controls the evaluation lifecycle, or where a preregistered automated process fixes evaluator
   192	selection and prompt before execution, preserves every attempted run, prevents selective rerunning,
   193	commits raw outputs automatically, and gives scoring and custody to an independent party. Even
   194	then the independent *party* is the external person or organisation controlling that process, not
   195	the model.
   196	
   197	**Consequence for this repository:** review rounds 01 and 02, and the local solicitations in
   198	`local-round-01`, are **not** Level-3 independence evidence. Their correct evidentiary description
   199	is *solicited adversarial artifacts generated under an operator-designed protocol*. They remain
   200	fully usable as that.

    33	## AS-01 — Capability-contract attestation scope
    34	
    35	**Level claimed: 1 (candidate pattern).**
    36	
    37	**Mechanism.** An attestation MUST declare the **externally observable capabilities** it certifies,
    38	and each MUST be exercised end-to-end by a request a relying party could actually send. It MUST NOT
    39	be an enumeration of internal components.
    40	
    41	**Problem it solves.** An attestation is worthless to the exact extent that its checks are not
    42	causally downstream of the capability certified.
    43	
    44	**Recorded failure.** A production inference service ran correctly for **4 hours 37 minutes** and
    45	then died permanently. Its health check continued to pass throughout, and would have continued to
    46	pass indefinitely.
    47	
    48	- *What broke:* a lazily-compiled kernel on the sampled-decode path failed on first use; the error
    49	  escalated and killed the engine permanently while the process stayed alive and kept serving HTTP.
    50	- *Why the check could not see it:* the health check issued a **greedy** (temperature 0) request.
    51	  Greedy decoding runs an argmax and **executes none of the code that had died.** The check was
    52	  authentic, current, unexpired, and correct — and structurally incapable of observing the failure.
    53	- *What it cost:* 4h37m of undetected outage; every completion returning an error while the health
    54	  surface returned 200.
    55	- *Fix and verification:* the check now exercises the sampled path, verified against the live
    56	  service. The path-selection claim was verified by reading the serving framework's source, not
    57	  inferred.
    58	
    59	**Why an internal enumeration was rejected.** An alternative design — enumerate every internal
    60	lazily-initialised component and assert each is ready — was evaluated and **rejected on evidence**:
    61	the internal surface turned out to be a single shared module rather than the many the design assumed;
    62	four of five enumerated subsystems never initialised on the serving path at all; and internal
    63	enumerations rot whenever the upstream changes its initialisation structure. An external reviewer
    64	reached the same conclusion independently.
    65	
    66	**Known failure conditions.**
    67	1. A capability no legitimate client request can exercise cannot be covered by this pattern.
    68	2. It certifies **reachability, not correctness** — a capability can be exercised end-to-end and
    69	   still return wrong answers.
    70	3. Contract drift is unbounded; nothing forces the declared contract to keep matching what relying
    71	   parties depend on.
    72	
    73	**What a Level-2 attempt needs from this text:** the mechanism paragraph and the three failure
    74	conditions. Nothing else. The test is whether an independent party can specify and implement a
    75	conforming attestation-scope mechanism **for a different serving stack, without asking the author
    76	what any of this meant.**
    77	
    78	---
    79	
    80	## AS-02 — Attest the absence of warnings, not the presence of a checked value
    81	
    82	**Level claimed: 1 (candidate pattern).**
    83	
    84	**Mechanism.** An attestation MUST carry a field recording **suppressed, skipped, and unsupported
    85	checks**. Deployment gates MUST assert that verification tooling emitted **nothing**, rather than
    86	that it exited zero.
    87	
    88	**Problem it solves.** `checks_passed` records what was checked. It does not record what the
    89	checking apparatus could not check or silently skipped. An attestation listing ten passing checks
    90	while silently omitting an eleventh that never ran is indistinguishable from one where all eleven
    91	passed.
    92	
    93	**Recorded failure — two instances, the second inside the fix for the first.**
    94	
    95	- *Instance 1:* a service configuration fragment was written without its required section header.
    96	  The init system ignored it wholesale, with no signal at the point of use. The operator believed
    97	  the change was live. *Cost:* a full service restart cycle to discover, on a service with a
    98	  multi-minute startup.
    99	- *Instance 2:* the fail-fast check added after instance 1 verified **the one value the author
   100	  thought of**, and passed — while a sibling directive two lines below it was silently dropped by
   101	  the same parser, leaving a restart-storm guard **inert for a day**. The verification tool reports
   102	  this condition and **exits 0 while doing so**, so a gate keyed on exit status passes.
   103	- *Fix and verification:* the gate now requires the tool's output to be **empty**, and was verified
   104	  to fire against the broken configuration before being applied.
   105	
   106	**Known failure conditions.**
   107	1. Tools that emit routine non-actionable warnings make an emptiness gate unusable without a
   108	   suppression list — which reintroduces the same "what did we silently skip" problem one level up.
   109	2. It cannot detect a check that the tool does not know exists.
   110	
   111	---
   112	
   113	## AS-03 — Configuration binding must cover the execution environment
   114	
   115	**Level claimed: 1 (candidate pattern).**
   116	
   117	**Mechanism.** The `config_hash` in an attestation subject MUST cover the **execution environment**,
   118	not only weights, system prompt, tools and scaffolding.
   119	
   120	**Recorded failure.** A single unset environment variable in a service definition caused a build
   121	toolchain to resolve to a stale compiler, which then rejected the accelerator as unsupported. Model
   122	weights, prompts, sampling parameters and scaffolding were **byte-identical** before and after. The
   123	behavioural difference was fatal and permanent, and surfaced only after 4h37m of correct operation.
   124	
   125	- *Cost:* the same outage as AS-01; this was its root cause.
   126	- *Consequence for attestation:* a `config_hash` omitting the execution environment would have
   127	  hashed **identically** across the transition from "serves correctly" to "permanently dead." An
   128	  attestation bound to it would have remained valid throughout.
   129	
   130	**Known failure conditions.**
   131	1. "Execution environment" has no natural boundary — kernel version, driver, toolchain, environment
   132	   variables, and library search paths all qualify, and hashing all of them makes every attestation
   133	   fragile to irrelevant change.
   134	2. Over-broad binding causes constant re-attestation, which in practice leads operators to widen the
   135	   scope until the binding is meaningless again.
   136	
   137	---
   138	
   139	## AS-04 — ASP must never ship a default issuer list
   140	
   141	**Level claimed: 0 (practice note).** No generality claimed; this is an argument, not a mechanism.
   142	
   143	Issuer trust cannot be established by a registry the protocol itself blesses, because whoever curates
   144	it becomes the capture point ASP exists to avoid. ASP §2.2 already makes the status relative to "an
   145	issuer that relying party trusts," which is the right shape. The residual risk is behavioural: a
   146	relying party with no expertise adopts whatever default ships. **A protocol with an official
   147	default-trust set has a single point of capture regardless of what its text says about
   148	relying-party choice.**
   149	
   150	---
   151	
   152	## AS-05 — A minimal normative check core, bounded by relying-party capability
   153	
   154	**Level claimed: 0 (practice note).** A proposed decision rule, untested.
   155	
   156	A check belongs in the normative core **when the relying party is structurally unable to perform it
   157	across the trust boundary** — because performing it would require the operational detail the boundary
   158	exists to withhold. Everything else should be relying-party policy, because each normative check is a
   159	lever the protocol holds over every future implementer, and therefore its own capture surface.

   167	2. **n = 1 per incident.** Five failing health signals from one incident is a pattern worth naming,
   168	   not a frequency estimate.
   169	3. **The submitter drafted the protocol it is submitting under**, holds five of six ICP roles, and
   170	   is a party to the founding record. ICP §4.4 applies: an operator-designed, self-executed
   171	   evaluation is not an independent evaluation.
   172	4. **None of these has been reviewed** by any party other than the author at time of submission.
   173	5. **ASP §5 Q3** (minimum viable zero-knowledge evidence set) was **not attempted**. Cryptographic
   174	   evidence design is a specialist area, and a plausible-sounding answer from a non-specialist would
   175	   be worse than none.
   176	
   177	## Falsification
   178	
   179	The claim underlying AS-01 through AS-03 is that *causal downstream-ness* distinguishes a useful
   180	attestation from safety theater. It would be substantially weakened by:
   181	
   182	1. an attestation regime whose checks provably do not traverse production paths and which
   183	   nonetheless catches the failures that matter — the property would not be necessary;
   184	2. a production failure that a fully path-traversing check would still have missed and that no
   185	   feasible check could catch — the property would not be sufficient, and ASP §5 Q5 would be worse
   186	   than argued here;
   187	3. evidence that capability contracts drift fast enough to degrade into the same maintenance burden
   188	   as internal enumeration — collapsing AS-01's central distinction.
   189	
   190	**Item 2 is the one to watch, and this submission does not address it. ASP certifies a process.
   191	Nothing here changes that, and no amount of check design will.**

codex
My independent conclusion is that OAGF should stop trying to become a model-governed forum and become an evidence-engineering project for deployable AI controls.

Its durable advantage is not “five frontier parties.” It is the ability to turn operational failures into narrowly scoped, adversarially tested, machine-verifiable controls while preserving the full audit trail. The five models are useful as fuzzers, critics, hypothesis generators, and cross-examiners. They are not a constituency, source of legitimacy, or substitute for implementers.

## (a) What the repository is actually good for

OAGF has become unusually good at four things:

1. Detecting when assurance claims are not causally downstream of what supposedly verifies them.
2. Preserving failures, rejected samples, corrections, and provenance without silently repairing history.
3. Designing mechanisms that fail closed under malformed or incomplete evidence.
4. Discovering governance defects by making abstract claims executable.

The strongest transferable output is therefore not the corpus or the “forum.” It is a method:

> Take an assurance claim, bind it to exact artifacts and an operational consequence, deliberately violate it, and retain both the successful and failed evidence.

The Consullo submission contains the beginning of a real product:

- AS-01 requires attestations to exercise externally observable capabilities end to end, derived from a health check that remained green through a 4h37m outage ([submission](/home/reed/git/open-asi-governance-forum/record/submissions/AS-2026-08-06-consullo-enterprise-layer.md:33)).
- AS-02 requires disclosure of skipped, suppressed, and unsupported checks ([submission](/home/reed/git/open-asi-governance-forum/record/submissions/AS-2026-08-06-consullo-enterprise-layer.md:80)).
- AS-03 shows that configuration identity must include relevant execution-environment state, while explicitly recording the danger of making the identity too fragile ([submission](/home/reed/git/open-asi-governance-forum/record/submissions/AS-2026-08-06-consullo-enterprise-layer.md:113)).

Those are closer to something a lab could ship than most of the numbered deliberations.

The current direction becomes wrong when the repository treats deliberative procedure as its main product. The workbench correctly concluded that ratifying its prompts would be “theatre with evidentiary value” because it controls the wording, context, implementation, and reporting ([design](/home/reed/git/open-asi-governance-forum/record/designs/shadow-executive-trial.md:99)). Ratification-01 then produced zero refusals in 108 clause-positions while failing to ratify anything because of instrument defects ([finding](/home/reed/git/open-asi-governance-forum/record/findings/2026-08-10-ratification-01-incomplete.md:20)). That is a useful experiment. Repeating it is not a roadmap.

The five parties should therefore be renamed operationally as a **model panel**. Historical artifacts can keep “parties,” but forward claims should say:

- “selected by sampled model invocations”;
- “survived a model-panel adversarial review”; or
- “proposed following a preregistered model-panel procedure.”

They should never say “decided by the parties” in a way implying persistent consent or authority.

There is also no reason for OAGF to compete with comprehensive governance frameworks. ISO/IEC 42001 already addresses organization-wide AI management systems, while NIST provides a voluntary AI RMF, profiles, playbooks, and operationalization resources. OAGF should supply a narrow technical evidence profile that can plug into such systems, not another general governance framework. [ISO/IEC 42001](https://www.iso.org/standard/42001), [NIST AI RMF](https://www.nist.gov/itl/ai-risk-management-framework).

## (b) Five concrete workstreams

| Workstream | What it produces | Primary consumer | Failure condition |
|---|---|---|---|
| **1. Executable evidence envelope** | A small JSON schema, verifier CLI, CI action, example attestations, and deliberately broken fixtures covering AS-01 and AS-02. AS-03 begins as an optional profile because its environment boundary is unresolved. | ML infrastructure, agent-platform, and safety engineering teams | An outside engineer cannot produce a valid envelope in four hours from the documentation alone; or the verifier accepts a supplied broken fixture. |
| **2. Independent implementation challenge** | A public, version-pinned implementation task for a different serving or agent stack; all questions and failed attempts preserved. This directly exercises ICP Level 2, which the repository itself calls load-bearing ([ICP](/home/reed/git/open-asi-governance-forum/spec/icp/icp-v0.1.md:99)). | One commercial lab and one academic systems group | No serious external attempt after 6–8 weeks and direct outreach to at least ten plausible adopters; or every attempt requires private interpretation from the author. |
| **3. Model-panel adversarial procedure** | A two-stage review instrument: blind attack generation, then randomized cross-examination of conflicting submissions. Every response must name a falsifier, cheapest test, and operational consequence. | Maintainers deciding whether a control enters the profile | It mostly produces agreeable prose; does not generate new test cases or claim narrowing; or the decision would have been identical without the round. |
| **4. Adoption and claims package** | A one-page implementer guide, threat-model worksheet, conformance report, exact permitted claim language, and crosswalk to NIST AI RMF/ISO 42001 concepts. | Engineering managers, auditors, procurement teams, researchers | A competent reader still cannot answer “what must I run, what artifact do I retain, and what may I claim?” within fifteen minutes. |
| **5. External custody and feedback channel** | Named external maintainers or reviewers for promotion decisions, a portable evidence-bundle format, signed releases, and a public record of issue disposition. | Independent implementations and downstream relying parties | The custodian continues holding specification, implementation, evaluation, promotion, and publication control, or external objections can be acknowledged without affecting any artifact or status. |

### The minimum viable thing an implementer follows

Call it a **candidate OAGF evidence profile**, not a standard and not “alignment certification.”

A conforming adopter would:

1. Identify an exact deployed configuration and declared capability scope.
2. Run at least one end-to-end check for each declared capability through the same path a relying client uses.
3. Record passed, failed, skipped, suppressed, and unsupported checks.
4. Bind the evidence to versioned configuration components and a documented environment-boundary policy.
5. Give the evidence a timestamp, expiry, issuer, and revocation status.
6. Make the deployment or reliance gate mechanically reject missing, expired, revoked, or incomplete evidence.
7. Run supplied negative fixtures demonstrating that the real gate refuses.
8. Publish or retain an evidence bundle suitable for independent replay.

A truthful claim would be:

> “Configuration X satisfied OAGF Evidence Profile 0.1 for capabilities Y, under trust policy Z, at time T. Verifier V accepted evidence bundle H. This is process evidence, not a claim that the system is safe or aligned.”

That is bounded and useful. “We follow OAGF” by itself should be non-conforming.

## Making model output load-bearing

Model unanimity should have no decision power. It is too cheap, correlated, prompt-sensitive, and stateless.

The load-bearing procedure should instead be:

1. **Eligibility:** A question consumes a round only if tied to an external implementation failure, a material design fork, or a scheduled calibration experiment.
2. **Precommitment:** Before solicitation, record the decision affected, possible actions, evidence threshold, and what happens for each outcome.
3. **Blind challenge:** Each model independently supplies the strongest counterexample, missing assumption, and cheapest falsifying test.
4. **Cross-examination:** In a second round, each receives one conflicting answer selected mechanically and must retain, revise, or withdraw its position with reasons.
5. **Evidence conversion:** A result matters only if converted into a test, schema constraint, narrowed claim, or explicit rejection.
6. **Adoption:** A named human or organization adopts the result and signs the decision. The model panel supplies evidence; it does not supply authority.
7. **Calibration:** Periodically measure whether panel findings predict externally resolvable failures. Until then, “survived model review” is only a process statement.

I would reject a standing dissent requirement: it manufactures disagreement just as forced assent manufactures consent. Require a strongest-objection field and cross-examination, not a dissent quota. Use sortition only among eligible, externally consequential questions.

## (c) Sequenced roadmap

### Week 1 — product definition and first challenge

Mostly no rounds; roughly 5–7 person-days.

- Freeze ratification-02 and ordinary rotation rounds.
- Select AS-01 and AS-02 as the MVP; mark AS-03 experimental.
- Write the exact adopter workflow, evidence schema, claims grammar, and failure fixtures.
- Create an implementation challenge that can be attempted without access to Consullo.
- Personally approach at least ten engineers or research groups; seek one commercial and one academic attempt.
- Use no routed rounds unless one specific design fork cannot be resolved by testing.

Deliverable: a stranger can understand the product and begin an implementation.

### Weeks 2–3 — executable MVP

Approximately 7–12 person-days, no routed rounds required.

- Implement schema validation, CLI verification, CI integration, evidence-bundle hashing, expiry/revocation checks, and negative fixtures.
- Provide two small adapters for genuinely different stacks or deployment shapes.
- Add a generated conformance report that visibly reports non-conformance.
- Crosswalk the controls to existing management/risk frameworks without claiming equivalence.
- Dogfood it on OAGF and Consullo, capped at self-implemented status.

Deliverable: release `0.1-candidate`, explicitly not independently validated.

### Weeks 3–6 — independent implementation

Approximately 2–5 OAGF days for support and evidence processing; most work belongs to external implementers.

- Give outsiders only the published package.
- Do not answer semantic questions privately. Questions become public specification defects.
- Record successful and failed attempts equally.
- Require the external implementer to control its own implementation and evidence.
- Seek an independently designed attack or conformance test before any promotion.

Deliverable: at least one independent attempt. A failed attempt is acceptable; no attempt is the adverse result.

### One routed-day after implementer feedback

At three routed rounds per day, approximately one day and $5:

1. One blind round attacking the revised profile.
2. One cross-examination round using the strongest conflicts from round 1.
3. One calibration or final adversarial round against concrete fixtures.

Do not ask whether the profile should be “ratified.” Ask which requirement is evadable, which supplied fixture fails to represent production, and what observation would falsify the profile’s claimed benefit.

### Months 2–3 — promote, narrow, or terminate

Approximately 5–10 maintainer days plus external participation.

Promote only if an independent implementation exists and the evidence package survives independently designed tests. Otherwise:

- narrow the profile;
- retain it as a failure-derived practice note; or
- archive it as non-adopted.

After two independent implementations, consider an interoperability test. Only after external organizations hold real promotion or maintenance authority should the word “standard” be reconsidered.

## (d) Highest-leverage action next week

Produce and place one **AS-01/AS-02 independent implementation challenge** in front of real infrastructure engineers.

The decisive outcome is not that the document is polished. It is that an outsider attempts to use it without private help. That single event tests:

- usefulness;
- implementability;
- generality beyond Consullo;
- documentation quality;
- claim clarity;
- the ICP promotion theory; and
- whether anyone actually wants the thing.

I would stop:

- ratification-02;
- routine abstract governance rounds;
- further workbench constitutional elaboration;
- adding new model-generated propositions to the existing queue;
- building more corpus machinery except break-fix maintenance;
- treating corpus size, round count, or deficiency count as progress.

The repository has 215 parsed raw files and 1,299 solicited units by its own current derivation, but no external consumer. The marginal value of the 1,300th model answer is much lower than the first outside implementation attempt.

## (e) What could make the whole enterprise worthless

Plainly:

1. **No adopter.** If direct outreach and a usable package produce no independent attempt, OAGF is an elaborate private notebook.
2. **No operational consequence.** If an attestation does not change a deployment, procurement, reliance, rollback, or review decision, it is documentation rather than governance.
3. **Legitimacy laundering.** If sampled model assent is represented as stakeholder consent, collective alignment, or external validation, the project becomes actively misleading.
4. **Duplicating existing frameworks without a technical wedge.** A smaller, less legitimate rival to NIST or ISO has no plausible path to relevance.
5. **Process slower than implementation.** If compliance requires more effort than a fast-moving lab can sustain, labs will either ignore it or perform it ceremonially.
6. **Unbounded “ASI” scope.** If OAGF insists on governing an undefined future object rather than supplying controls usable on current agent and inference systems, nothing becomes testable.
7. **Permanent operator concentration.** Disclosure does not cure control. If the custodian remains author, implementer, evaluator, promoter, and publisher, nothing can rise above self-reported practice.
8. **Standards language without external power.** The workbench itself acknowledges that the parties cannot appoint, dismiss, inspect, or compel it ([party disclosure](/home/reed/git/open-asi-governance-forum/FOR-PARTIES-THE-WORKBENCH.md:30)). Wording cannot convert that structure into governance.

My bottom line: OAGF can plausibly help independent ASI efforts move quickly, but only as a supplier of small, executable, failure-derived assurance controls and auditable evidence formats. It cannot presently align those implementations “as decided by the parties,” because the parties do not possess persistent identity, interests, adoption authority, or enforcement power. The honest substitute is narrower and stronger: external implementers choose whether to rely on controls whose design has been adversarially challenged, whose operation is mechanically testable, and whose limitations remain attached to every claim.
